title: Parker, Clifford Brown, Lester Young and Armstrong solos

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: published legally, you can buy it in any music store. Good transcriptions. And I think that's one thing they should learn.

I don't care what instrument you play, any instrument should learn Charlie Parker's solos. And his pieces, that's "Moose the Mooche" part of the repertoire, you've got to know and "Confirmation" and "Donna Lee," and all those -- you know, they call them "heads," I guess, the melodic -- you know, the written out part of the solo. And then you learn the ad lib solo. But I think that all instruments should learn those solos.

There are some classic Freddie Hubbard solos, some classic Clifford Brown solos, "Donna Lee," Clifford Brown solo on "Confirmation" that he made with Max Roach. That's a classic. You could spend six months on that solo, a trumpet player could, and I think any other instrument. Because I don't think that any instrument should stick to its own instrument, because each instrument's got its mechanical limitations.
No, no, this is what I want.

And, you know, a trumpet player will play what's easy for the trumpet. So you're not going to branch out too far. But if you play saxophone solos and piano solos, nowadays piano solos are good because they play single line solos, they play like a horn now. It's not easy on the trumpet and you develop techniques. But you also get ideas and perspec-

tives that you wouldn't get just with the trumpet.
Now, I wish that solos -- you take Lester Young's solos, they've not been published, and I think that's another -- mostly the solos he did with Basie, I feel those are his best solos. But God knows, he made enough. They're putting out Lester Young stories, about seven albums out now, I think. Unfortunately, not all of them are good, but the stuff with Basie is the best. And there's two albums of that. And you should learn those solos. Even if they were written out they wouldn't do you much good because that's a feeling that you really have to learn.
And the same thing with Louis, don't you think so?

That's a feeling. You can learn -- Louis's notes with the Hot Five, those are notes you can learn, but after the Hot Five, it was no longer a matter of technical -- there was just a -- I feel that's when he really blossomed out into singing. And that's a feeling. You should learn the notes and where he placed them, but that's not going to do you any good except as far as your fingers are concerned. If you don't get the feeling. You've got to get the feeling.
